BUILD-4.title: Tests pass
BUILD-4.requires: Node 22; `test-ci`, not `test`, because `nx test` hangs locally

refs.POA-D3: A `Database` variant of `RoutingPolicySourceSpec`, added alongside `None`/`Inline`/`File`/`Gcs`, not replacing them.
refs.POA-D4: An unconfigured `(model, feature)` has no projected entry and routes by the existing default precedence, reported as `'default-precedence'`.
refs.POA-D7: Apply is a whole-document, single-transaction, optimistically-concurrent write keyed on the stored configuration's revision. Zero enabled providers is a legal "do not serve" state that fails the pair with a typed error.
refs.POA-D8: Generic `dryRun: 'succeed' | 'fail'`, short-circuiting before any provider HTTP call and any wallet debit.
refs.POA-D9: Attribution (provider + `RoutingSource` + `policyHash` + dry-run flag) is persisted, logged, metered and returned, including over MCP.
refs.POA-R1: The serve-nothing set travels inside the policy document: the router sees only the `PolicySnapshot`'s document, and `routingPolicyHash` covers only the document.
refs.POA-R2: The Apply path and the background poller are two independent writers of `RoutingPolicyService`; the swap must refuse a document whose revision is older than the one in force.
refs.POA-R4: `generation_history.asset_id` references `assets`, so a dry run, which has no asset, records its attribution in a separate `routing_decisions` table.
refs.POA-A3.b: The dry-run short-circuit sits in `candidate-execution.ts`, so the attempt record is produced exactly as a live call produces it.
refs.EFF-10: Domain failures are typed errors in the error channel (`Data.TaggedError`), never thrown, never `Effect.die` for an expected refusal.
refs.EFF-32: No read-then-write across a `yield*` where an invariant spans it; the existing `Ref.modify` compare-and-swap is the reference.

tasks.title: Implement services — source, routing semantics, dry run, attribution
tasks.goal: Phase 2. The behaviour changes. Each subtask preserves a named property of the `provider-routing` workstream.

tasks.title: Add the `Database` routing-policy source variant
tasks.goal: Let the live policy come from the table without teaching the policy service anything new.
tasks.approach: Extend **every** `$match` — the exhaustive matcher failing to compile is the intended safety net, not an obstacle. The source offers documents through the existing `load`, so the "a rejected replacement never removes the working policy" property is inherited rather than re-implemented.

touches.what: a `Database` case on `RoutingPolicySourceSpec`; `specUri` renders it as `db://routing-config`

tasks.title: Wire source selection, polling and load semantics
tasks.goal: Make the database the selectable source, and prove the existing load properties still hold when reached through it.
tasks.approach: **Finding POA-R2:** the Apply path and the background poller are two independent writers of `RoutingPolicyService`. Without a revision comparison in the swap, a poll in flight across an Apply silently reverts the administrator's change for up to one poll interval — after they were told it succeeded. The swap must therefore refuse an older revision, not merely a matching hash.

touches.what: extend `routingPolicySourceSpecConfig` so the source is selected by configuration
the compare-and-swap refuses a document whose revision is older than the one in force (POA-R2)

tasks.title: Update the router so a pair configured to serve nothing is not treated as unconfigured
tasks.goal: Make a deliberately-emptied pair fail loudly instead of silently reverting to the built-in default.
tasks.approach: This is the one genuine semantic change to `provider-router.ts`. Today an absent entry and a serve-nothing entry are indistinguishable; after this they must not be. Add a tagged failure alongside the existing `NoCandidateSatisfiesConstraints` rather than reusing it — the operator response differs completely ("your constraints excluded everything" versus "you switched everything off").

touches.what: a pair configured with zero enabled providers fails with a new typed error instead of falling through to default precedence

tasks.title: Add the dry-run mode to the gateway
tasks.goal: Let a caller ask "who would serve this?" and get a truthful answer without a provider call or a charge.
tasks.approach: Extend the input of `deriveIdempotencyKey` so the mode is part of the key: a dry run must neither collide with nor poison a live call's idempotency key.

notHere.what: the short-circuit itself — this task supplies the mode and the money guarantee

tasks.title: Move the dry-run short-circuit to the attempt boundary so attribution is shape-identical
tasks.goal: Make a dry run produce the *same* attribution record a live call produces — which is the entire reason a dry run can be used as proof.
tasks.approach: Placing the short-circuit here rather than higher in the gateway is what buys the shape-identity (POA-A3.b); the "no adapter entered" property is preserved and separately asserted.

touches.what: the short-circuit sits after the candidate is chosen and before the provider adapter is entered, where the attempt record is still produced

tasks.title: Write the routing-decision record and the generation attribution
tasks.goal: Make it impossible for a generation to exist without a record of why the provider that served it was chosen.
tasks.approach: Extend the existing `recordGeneration` input rather than adding a second write path for the generation half — the atomicity guarantee in the `0015` migration docblock depends on there being exactly one. The routing-decision record is a separate, additional write that every call makes, live or dry (POA-R4). Regenerate the DB types after T1.1 with `pnpm nx run db:codegen`.

touches.what: extend the existing `recordGeneration` input, and add the routing-decision write that every call makes, live or dry

scenarios.title: Switching a provider off removes it from consideration entirely
steps: Given a model whose ordering names two enabled providers
When an administrator switches the first provider off and applies the change
And a request for that model is then made
Then the remaining enabled provider serves the request
And the switched-off provider is not asked at all, even when the remaining provider fails

scenarios.title: A model with no stored ordering routes by the built-in default
steps: Given a model with no stored provider ordering
When a request for that model is made
Then it is served by the built-in default preference
And the recorded decision states that the built-in default was the source of the choice

scenarios.title: A model whose providers are all switched off refuses to serve, distinguishably
steps: Given a model whose ordering exists but has every provider switched off
When a request for that model is made
Then the request fails with a reason that names the model and says it is configured to serve nothing
And that failure is distinguishable from the case where the model has no stored ordering at all

scenarios.title: A dry run that is asked to succeed reports the provider it would have used
steps: Given a model with a stored provider ordering
When a caller makes a request in dry-run mode asking for a successful outcome
Then the response is a success
And it names the provider that a real request would have gone to
And the result is unambiguously marked as not being a real generation

scenarios.title: A dry run that is asked to fail produces a failure without contacting anyone
steps: Given a model with a stored provider ordering
When a caller makes a request in dry-run mode asking for a failing outcome
Then the request fails in the same way a real provider failure would present
And the provider that would have been used is still recorded

scenarios.title: A dry run contacts no provider
steps: Given a model with a stored provider ordering
When a caller makes a request in dry-run mode
Then no provider is contacted
And no external call is made on the caller's behalf

scenarios.title: A malformed submission is refused and the previous configuration keeps serving
steps: Given a stored provider ordering that is currently in force
When an administrator submits a configuration that cannot be understood
Then the submission is refused with a reason
And the previously-stored ordering is still the one in force

scenarios.title: A submission naming an unknown provider is refused, naming every unknown one
steps: Given a submission that names providers the system has nothing registered for
When it is applied
Then it is refused
And the refusal names every unrecognised provider, not merely the first

scenarios.title: When the configuration store cannot be reached the last good configuration keeps serving
steps: Given a configuration that has been loaded and is in force
When the configuration store becomes unreachable
Then requests continue to be routed by the configuration already in force
And the operational surface reports that the newest read did not succeed

scenarios.title: A failing first provider hands over to the next switched-on provider
steps: Given a model whose ordering names three providers, the second of which is switched off
And the first provider fails in a way that permits another to be tried
When a request for that model is made
Then the third provider serves it
And the switched-off second provider was never asked

scenarios.title: A refused configuration never disturbs the one that is serving
steps: Given a configuration in force
When a replacement is offered and refused for any reason
Then the configuration in force is byte-for-byte the one that was serving before
And its identity is unchanged

scenarios.title: What served a request is recorded together with the request's outcome
steps: Given a request that results in a generation
Then the provider that served it, the reason that provider was chosen, and the identity of the configuration in force are recorded as part of the same indivisible record as the generation itself
And there is no state in which the generation exists without them
And the same facts are also recorded as a routing decision in their own right, so a request that produces no artefact is still accounted for

scenarios.title: An operator can see where the live configuration came from and whether the latest read worked
steps: Given a running service reading its configuration from the store
When an operator inspects the operational surface
Then it states which source the configuration in force came from
And whether the most recent read of that source succeeded or was refused

scenarios.title: A configuration change landing mid-request does not change that request
steps: Given a request that has begun and has already resolved which provider to use
When the configuration is replaced while that request is still running
Then the request completes against the provider it originally resolved
And a request begun afterwards uses the replacement

scenarios.title: Re-applying an identical configuration is not treated as a change
steps: Given a stored configuration
When an administrator applies a configuration that is equivalent to the one already in force
Then it is accepted
And it is reported as unchanged rather than as a new configuration

scenarios.title: The previously-supported configuration sources continue to work
steps: Given a deployment configured to read its routing configuration from its existing external source
When the service starts and polls that source
Then it loads and serves that configuration exactly as it did before this feature existed

scenarios.title: A caller who says nothing about dry runs is unaffected
steps: Given a caller that makes a request without mentioning dry runs
When the request is made
Then it behaves exactly as it did before dry runs existed, including being charged

scenarios.title: A caller that records a generation without the new detail still succeeds
steps: Given a caller that records a generation without stating the provider, the reason, or the configuration identity
When the generation is recorded
Then it is recorded successfully
And the absent details are stored as absent rather than as invented values

scenarios.title: Models nobody has configured behave exactly as before
steps: Given a deployment upgraded to this feature with no configuration stored at all
When requests are made across the catalogue
Then every model is served exactly as it was before the upgrade

scenarios.title: The deployed service reads its configuration from the store
steps: Given the service deployed to its hosting environment with the configuration store selected as its source
When it starts
Then it loads the stored configuration
And routes requests by it

environment.setup: the service deployed to its hosting environment, with the configuration store selected

scenarios.title: A dry run costs nothing
steps: Given a caller with a known balance
When they make a dry-run request, whether asked to succeed or to fail
Then their balance is unchanged
And no charge is created

scenarios.title: A dry run is recorded in the same shape as a real request
steps: Given a real request and a dry-run request for the same model
Then the record of what served each is the same shape, carrying the same fields
And the only difference is that one is marked as a dry run
And that sameness is what makes a dry run usable as proof of what a real request would do

scenarios.title: A model configured to serve nothing is part of the configuration's identity
steps: Given two configurations that are identical except that one has a model configured to serve nothing
Then they are not treated as the same configuration
And the routing layer can tell, for any model, whether it is configured to serve nothing
And that fact reaches the routing layer by the same route as the ordering itself, not by a separate channel

scenarios.title: A slow read cannot undo a change that has already been applied
steps: Given a periodic read of the stored configuration that began before an administrator applied a change
When that read completes after the change has taken effect
Then it does not replace the newer configuration with the older one
And the administrator's change is still the one in force

scenarios.title: A request that produces nothing still records which provider it would have used
steps: Given a dry-run request, which creates no artefact and no charge
Then the provider it resolved to, the reason, and the identity of the configuration in force are recorded
And that record is readable afterwards without reference to any artefact
And it is marked as a dry run so it can never be mistaken for real work

scenarios.title: A stored configuration naming a provider that cannot serve the model is refused
steps: Given a stored configuration naming a provider that is known to the system but cannot serve the model in question
When that configuration is read
Then it is refused
And the refusal names every such provider, not merely the first
And the configuration already in force keeps serving
